Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: Revenue collection is supported via DGI's online tax declaration and payment system (STT), which enables taxpayers to pay taxes online ([DGI Mauritania](https://impots.gov.mr/DGI/teleservices.html)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed that DGI's STT portal (stt.e-tax.impots.gov.mr) allows online tax declaration and payment. However, the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement Database (accessed 2026) still lists electronic payment of import/export duties as an unimplemented commitment with 'no progress reported', contradicting a secondary trade-blog claim that customs is now digital-only. As the variable covers taxes AND customs duties, and customs e-payment is unconfirmed by an authoritative source, downgraded from 3 (Yes) to 2 (Partial: tax payment confirmed digital, customs duties not corroborated as digitally payable).

Definition: Whether an official government web portal or mobile application exists where taxpayers can file tax returns and pay taxes online with direct e-payment capability linked to instant payment system.
Comments: Mauritania's DGI operates a tax portal for e-filing and e-payment (“Système de télédéclaration et télépaiement (STT)”) accessible at stt.e-tax.impots.gov.mr and references an additional tele-services portal (tele-services.gov.mr) ([DGI Mauritania](https://impots.gov.mr/DGI/teleservices.html)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed directly on the official DGI site: the STT portal (stt.e-tax.impots.gov.mr) supports both online tax declaration and payment, with a further teleservices portal (tele-services.gov.mr) for account/document management. Score of 4 (Yes) is well supported by this primary, authoritative source; no change.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system enables or plans to enable instant payments across national borders to other countries or regional payment systems, supporting remittances, trade, and regional integration.
Comments: Cross-border payments are described as supported through connections between the Mauritania National Switch and regional systems, enabling faster settlement and low-cost international transfers through banks/fintech/mobile networks; however, no formal regional instant-payment linkage (e.g., PAPSS participation) could be confirmed, so this is scored as partially functional ([TransFi](https://www.transfi.com/blog/mauritanias-payment-rails-how-they-work---national-switch-e-banking-mobile-wallet-expansion)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate. Comment wording may not match the score — re-read (needs judgement).
revision_notes: The sole original source was a generic, non-specific marketing blog (TransFi) whose own comment already flagged a mismatch. A current (June 2026) PAPSS network coverage document lists live participants and extended-network countries and Mauritania appears in neither list, indicating no confirmed regional instant cross-border payment linkage. The 2026 US ITA fintech guide confirms only that GIMTEL (the national switch) was certified in the Visa Global Registry in 2025 — international card-network interoperability, not an instant cross-border payment system. No authoritative evidence of even a planned instant cross-border linkage was found, so downgraded from 4 (Partially functional) to 1 (No). Flagged for human review given the definitional boundary between card-network interoperability and instant payment cross-border functionality.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: A World Bank–supported initiative commissioned a framing/feasibility study aimed at digitizing government payments in Mauritania, including a deployment roadmap and specifications for a payment platform, indicating limited/under-development G2P digitization rather than fully mature nationwide use ([Sofrecom](https://www.sofrecom.com/en/news-insights/digitization-of-payments-in-mauritania.html)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Corroborated: the Tekavoul national social transfer programme already disburses quarterly cash transfers to over 200,000 poor households (including refugee households) via smart payment cards and agent networks (World Bank, 2024), showing existing but programme-specific digitisation, while the 2024 Sofrecom/World Bank study confirms a separate, still-nascent effort to build a government-wide G2P digital payment platform. This supports 'Limited Use' rather than 'Yes - Active Use'; score of 2 confirmed unchanged.

Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed unchanged, now on stronger evidence.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Mauritania adopted a law related to electronic payment services in June 2021, intended to create an enabling regulatory environment and expand access to low-value transactional payment services ([UNCDF Policy Accelerator](https://policyaccelerator.uncdf.org/whats-new/mauritania-regulatory-framework)). The same source implies consumer protection remains a work-in-progress, so this is scored as partial rather than a comprehensive payments consumer protection regime.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Corroborated with the primary legal source: Law No. 2021-014 on electronic payment services and means (112 articles across 4 sections, replacing Ordinance 036-2006) is confirmed via the Ministry of Digitalisation's official legal register, alongside the general Law No. 2020-007 on consumer protection (FAOLEX). Neither text could be confirmed to set out payment-specific liability allocation, disclosure or dispute-resolution rules in detail, so 'Partial' (2) is retained; a dedicated, comprehensive payments consumer-protection regime is not evidenced.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Mauritania has a general personal data protection framework via Law No. 2017-020 (protection of personal data), establishing a personal data protection authority (APD) ([Data Protection Africa](https://dataprotection.africa/mauritania/)). This is general privacy legislation rather than payment-data-specific provisions.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Corroborated: UNCTAD's 2024 e-commerce readiness assessment for Mauritania confirms the country has adopted laws on electronic transactions, cybercrime, personal data protection and electronic payment means, consistent with the Data Protection Africa factsheet on Law No. 2017-020 and its data protection authority (APD). No payment-specific data provisions were found in either source, so 'General Data Protection Legislation' (2) is confirmed unchanged.

Definition: Whether independent external audits of payment system security, operations, financial controls, and compliance are conducted by third-party auditors, and whether audit results or summaries are made public.
Comments: An external audit report exists for Banque Centrale de Mauritanie (BCM) IFRS financial statements as of 31 Dec 2023, providing public independent audit evidence ([BCM audit report (IFRS 2023)](https://rimbyreports.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/rapport_audit_et_maquette_des_etats_financiers_ifrs_au_31_12_2023_final_17df49d78f.pdf)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Fetched and confirmed the cited document is a KPMG-Tunisia independent auditor's report on BCM's IFRS financial statements for FY2023, publicly posted — but it is a general central bank financial-statement audit, not an audit specifically of the payment system's security, operations or compliance as the variable requires. A separate search found the BCM-chaired Conseil des Systèmes de Paiement (payment systems oversight council) meets and discusses security/resilience, but no dedicated payment-system audit report was located. Evidence only partially matches the variable definition; left the value unchanged and flagged for human review rather than asserting a score change on a mismatched single source.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: AFI's case study notes initiatives to improve refugees' access to financial services (e.g., collaboration with the Djikké cooperative for urban refugees), but describes digitization/mobile money as still limited/infant, implying only partial access rather than broad inclusion ([AFI case study](https://www.afi-global.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/AFI_FDPs_CS_MAURITANIA_FINAL.pdf)).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Corroborated: the World Bank's Sahel Adaptive Social Protection Programme confirms that over 18,000 refugee/host households are supported through the Tekavoul digital cash-transfer programme, with payments to refugee households in Nouakchott beginning in 2024 (30,317 households as of reporting). This shows targeted, programme-specific inclusion rather than blanket access to mainstream digital payment accounts, consistent with 'Partial' (2); score confirmed unchanged.
